source_metadata.title: Agent Memory Distillation: Empowering Small LLM Agents with Hierarchical Teacher Memory
source_metadata.source_type: arXiv preprint; primary empirical AI/agent-systems study
source_metadata.scope: All 25 pages inspected. Main text, quantitative tables, figures with load-bearing numeric results, algorithmic appendix, robustness analyses, and stated limitations were considered. Bibliographic references were not atomized as evidence.

validated_atoms.canonical_statement: The study investigates whether structured teacher memory can be transferred without parameter training to improve small 4B–8B language-model agents on multi-turn tool-use tasks despite a teacher–student capability gap.
AMD constructs its memory store only from successful teacher trajectories and partitions the resulting knowledge into Workflow, Subtask, and Function memory banks.

Workflow memory summarizes high-level task strategy, including tools, preconditions, decision rules, validation cues, and common failure patterns, while replacing runtime-specific values with typed placeholders.
Subtask memory segments each successful teacher trajectory into semantically coherent units and stores concrete execution examples with a short label and description for each segment.
Function memory stores function-level invocation examples with surrounding context and, when available, API documentation describing argument and response schemas.
AMD pre-encodes memory entries and uses cosine-similarity retrieval with a minimum similarity threshold for memory selection.
Workflow memory is retrieved using the task instruction and injected into the system prompt before the student issues any tool calls.

Before execution, the student decomposes a task into at most six ordered subtask labels; each label retrieves a best-matching Subtask memory entry, with deduplication across subtasks before proactive prompt injection.

Function memory is injected reactively after a tool-call error: candidate records are looked up by failing function name, ranked by similarity to the current task, and appended as targeted corrective hints.

The main experiments used GPT-5-mini as teacher; Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, Gemma4-E4B, and Llama3.1-8B as students; text-embedding-3-small for retrieval; k=1 for each memory type; and two repeated runs whose average performance was reported.
Student agents were allowed at most 40 interaction steps per task; Qwen3 thinking mode was disabled, students were served with vLLM, and the GPT-5-mini teacher was queried through the OpenAI API.

To test whether gains depended on memory derived from the evaluation task itself, the authors used a 7:3 cross-split protocol and a self-excluded retrieval protocol in which each task could retrieve only memories distilled from other tasks.
Run-to-run robustness was assessed by repeating the zero-shot and AMD configurations five times with Qwen3-4B under the same experimental setup.
The AppWorld evaluation used the 168-task test_normal subset, where agents interact with simulated applications through Python API calls and success is measured by database-state unit tests.
The BFCL V3 evaluation used the 200-task multi-turn base subset; a task is correct only when every turn matches the expected API state and a minimal viable call path.
The ToolSandbox evaluation used 129 base scenarios with JSON tool calls, a shared world state, GPT-5-mini as the simulated user, and scoring against human-authored milestones and minefields.

AMD is a hierarchical teacher-memory intervention combining Workflow memory for planning, Subtask memory for concrete intermediate execution examples, and Function memory for reactive function-call correction.
The study compared AMD with zero-shot students and with ReasoningBank, MemP, and SASM adapted to teacher-to-student transfer using the same teacher trajectories.

validated_atoms.canonical_statement: In the AppWorld Venmo case study, Workflow memory corrected the current-month scope, Subtask memory supplied a working date-parsing pattern, and Function memory corrected balance-response parsing; the full hierarchy completed the task after the less complete configurations failed at successive stages.

The authors conclude that effective teacher-to-student memory transfer for small agents requires hierarchical organization across planning, subtask execution, and function-call guidance, with memory complexity aligned to student capacity.
AMD was evaluated only on text-based tool-use benchmarks with Python APIs or structured function calls; generalization to multimodal environments and open-ended coding tasks was not tested.

AMD constructs memory offline from a fixed set of teacher trajectories and keeps it frozen at inference, so it cannot incorporate student successes or failures at test time or adapt to distribution shifts.

AMD depends on the quality and suitability of teacher trajectories, and the authors report that a stronger teacher does not always produce larger student gains because teacher–student compatibility also matters.

extraction_limitations: The current LiteratureAtom schema has no dedicated fields for benchmark identity, model architecture, standard deviation, computational cost, or agent-memory structures; these were preserved in population labels, exposure details, original_result_text, and tags where defensible.
Standard deviations in the five-run robustness table are preserved as source text because the schema interval object does not represent standard deviation.
No funding disclosure, conflict-of-interest statement, or data-availability statement was atomized because no such statement was identified in the inspected paper text.
Bibliographic citations and related-work claims were not extracted as primary evidence atoms.
